articles.title: Chad: Cholera Outbreak - DREF Final Report (MDRTD026)
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Description of the Event Date when the trigger was met 15-09-2025 What happened, where and when? The cholera outbreak in Chad began with a suspected case notified on 13 July 2025 in Chokoyane Health District (Ouaddaï Province). Vibrio cholerae O1 Ogawa was confirmed by culture on 24 July, and the Ministry of Public Health and Prevention officially declared the outbreak on 25 July. Cross-border transmission from Darfur (Sudan) is considered the most likely source. The Chad Red Cross (CRT) monitored the situation from the declaration onwards. Initially concentrated in Ouaddaï (Chokoyane, Hadjer Hadid, Adré), the outbreak escalated sharply in early September. Cases rose from 1,891 on 9 September to 2,165 cases and 137 deaths (CFR 6.3%) on 18 September. Community mortality remained high. By midSeptember, the outbreak was active in 8 districts across 3 provinces: five in Ouaddaï (Chokoyane, Hadjer Hadid, Adré, Farchana, Amleyouna), two in Sila (Abdi, Goz Beïda) and one in Guéra (Bitkine). Under the National Response Plan, the Government called on partners for support and prepositioning. CRT was asked to help contain the geographical spread and reduce community-level mortality. The DREF trigger was met on 15 September 2025, and the operation started on 23 September. During the operation, transmission declined in the initial hotspots. The last cases were notified in Hadjer Hadid on 21 September, Adré on 26 September, Abéché on 29 September, Abdi on 1 October and Chokoyane on 7 October. Weekly new cases fell from about 270 in midSeptember to about 30 from mid-October onwards. However, the outbreak continued to spread westward with population movements. It reached Amdam, Marfa and Abougoudam (Ouaddaï), Tissi (Sila), and from October Hadjer Lamis (Bokoro, Massaguet, Gama, Moyto) and Barh El Gazel (Moussoro). Bitkine (Guéra) became the second-largest focus, with 437 cases. The last confirmed case was notified on 19 November 2025 in Amdam. As of 7 December, the cumulative total was 2,979 cases and 167 deaths (CFR 5.61%), across 18 districts and 98 health areas in 5 provinces. 95% of patients recovered. The Ministry declared the end of the outbreak on 15 December 2025. In line with its post-epidemic recommendations, CRT, with IFRC support, reoriented its remaining activities towards community-based surveillance, RCCE and hygiene promotion until the end of the operation on 31 March 2026.

articles.title: ICYMI: ADNOC denies report of third Hormuz bypass pipeline that could open to other producers
articles.description: A shared bypass line would chip away at the Hormuz risk premium over time by giving Gulf producers beyond the UAE a route to market that avoids the strait. With ADNOC’s denial, though, the report is unlikely to move crude near term, and the risk premium stays anchored to shipping attacks and transit volumes through the strait itself. The 2027 second line is the more tangible supply factor, potentially easing Asian buyers’ exposure to Hormuz disruption. Repeated attacks on Fujairah also limit how much comfort traders can take from bypass capacity, keeping the infrastructure itself part of the risk. - The pipeline ADNOC says isn’t happening would have turned the UAE from a country avoiding Hormuz into one selling a way around it. Summary: Bloomberg reported ADNOC is weighing a third pipeline from the UAE’s west coast to Fujairah, bypassing Hormuz The line could be open to third parties and was described to some Asian customers, but plans are not final ADNOC called the report inaccurate and purely speculative An existing line carries about 2 million barrels a day, and a second line due in 2027 would roughly double capacity The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are all pursuing ways to reduce reliance on the strait Fujairah and Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline have both been attacked during the war Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. has denied a report that it is weighing a third crude pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, a project that, according to Bloomberg, could be opened to other producers and turn the UAE’s east coast into a wider export outlet for Gulf oil. Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter, that ADNOC was considering a new line from the UAE’s western coast to the port of Fujairah, which sits outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman. The pipeline could be made available to third parties, and ADNOC had described the plan to some Asian customers, the report said, adding that the project was not finalised and its route could change. No cost or timeline was given. ADNOC told Bloomberg the report was inaccurate and purely speculative. The third-party element is what sets the report apart from the UAE’s existing bypass strategy. ADNOC already operates a pipeline from its western onshore fields to Fujairah with capacity of about 2 million barrels a day, according to Bloomberg, and said in May it was accelerating a second line due for completion in 2027 that would roughly double that capacity. Both serve ADNOC’s own exports. A line open to other shippers would instead position Fujairah as a regional route around Hormuz, extending the UAE’s reach beyond its own production. That would fit the direction the UAE has taken since leaving OPEC in May, with plans to invest in pipelines, rail, roads and at least three eastern ports to reduce its reliance on the strait. Neighbours are moving the same way: Saudi Arabia plans to expand its East-West pipeline, and Kuwait is in talks with both countries about alternative routes. The backdrop explains the urgency. Hormuz was almost shut at the height of the Iran war, and while traffic has picked up, ships are still frequently targeted. Bypass routes are not immune either. Fujairah has been attacked several times during the conflict, and Saudi Arabia’s East-West line was briefly halted after an attack in September. With ADNOC rejecting the report, the plan remains unconfirmed. The more concrete milestone for oil markets is the second pipeline, which ADNOC has told some Asian refiners could supply cargoes at Fujairah from early 2027. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Mozambique learns from Japan’s expertise in disaster risk reduction
articles.description: How can countries invest today to reduce disaster losses tomorrow? A delegation from Mozambique explored this question during a study tour and workshop in Japan, learning how centuries of experience, strategic investment and technological innovation can help reduce disaster risks and strengthen resilience. Mozambique faces recurring cyclones, floods, droughts and storm surges that continue to threaten lives, livelihoods and critical infrastructure. As the country works to strengthen its disaster risk reduction mechanisms, representatives led by the National Institute for Disaster Management and Risk Reduction (INGD), supported by Ministry of Finance and Eduardo Mondlane University embarked on a study tour to Nagoya, Japan. The study tour took place from 5 to 9 October 2026. Organized by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) in collaboration with Tohoku University and funded by the Government of Japan, which is part of the project Strengthening Readiness for Resilient Recovery and Build Back Better in Mozambique. The study tour included visits to flood-prone communities in Kaizu, Gifu Prefecture, where participants explored both historical and modern approaches to flood risk management. At Inuyama Castle and the Waju Pumping Station, delegates learned how centuries of local knowledge, combined with substantial investment in flood protection infrastructure, have helped communities live with recurring flood hazards. Participants also visited the Storm Surge Protection Embankment Seismic Reinforcement Site in Kisosaki town, Mie Prefecture. The reinforcement site enables countermeasures for earthquake and tsunami risks, further demonstrating the value of continuous improvement of existing DRR measures. Additionally, participants learned about other measures to improve storm surge protections at Nagoya Port. Between 2013 and 2016, the Nagoya Port and Airport Office completed an improvement project to strengthen the port’s sea wall. The seawall was equipped with two lines of protection. These pre-emptive improvements have enabled better protection in anticipation of future earthquakes and tsunamis. “We designed a program focusing on the evolution of Japan’s disaster risk reduction capabilities — from before the country's modernization, through the modernization process itself, and particularly on how our predecessors engaged in trial and error following large-scale disasters. The participants were highly motivated, and the question-and-answer sessions were lively. The program proved to be a meaningful experience for all involved." - Professor Yuichi Ono, Tohoku University A key message throughout the study tour was that engineering solutions alone cannot eliminate disaster risk. Japan's experience showed the value of combining structural measures, such as drainage systems and coastal defences, with non-structural measures like land-use planning, early warning systems, evacuation planning and public awareness programmes. A large contributing factor also proved to be coordination between governing bodies. Public authorities, port operators and private-sector partners worked together to support preparedness, protect investments and ensure business continuity during disasters was also highlighted. Akio Tomita, Deputy Director-General of the Ports and Airports Department, for the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism shared three key messages for the delegation: “Plan for risks before disasters happen, combine hard and soft measures, and build partnerships before a crisis.” Private-sector companies Weathernews Inc. and Gaia Vision demonstrated how weather forecasting, flood modelling and risk assessment tools can help decision-makers better understand hazard exposure and potential impacts. These tools can support investment planning by identifying vulnerable populations, critical infrastructure and economic assets at risk. Combined with local data and cost-benefit analysis, such information can help governments prioritize investments that deliver long-term social and economic benefits. By combining historical knowledge, risk-informed investments, technological innovation and multi-stakeholder partnerships, Japan demonstrates how sustained investment in resilience can reduce disaster losses and support long-term development. As Mozambique continues to advance efforts to build back better and strengthen readiness for future disasters, the exchange highlighted the value of international cooperation and peer learning in accelerating progress towards a more resilient future. "The study tour to Japan provided a deeper understanding of the importance of an integrated and sustainable approach to disaster risk reduction. Going forward, Mozambique's goal is to adapt these lessons to our own national context rather than directly replicating the Japanese model. It will be essential to strengthen coordination among key disaster risk reduction institutions, alongside the finance sector and other relevant stakeholders, with the goal of creating an integrated information base covering risks, losses and damages, exposure, and vulnerability." - Rita Almeida, Director of Planning and Cooperation, INGD, Mozambique
